cards.front: What is information visualisation concerned with?
cards.back: Showing quantitative and qualitative information so viewers can see patterns, trends, anomalies, constancy, or variation more easily than with text or tables.

cards.front: According to Stephen Few, what are the two broad purposes of data visualisation?
cards.back: Sense-making/data analysis and communication.

cards.front: According to Card et al., what does information visualisation use visual representations to do?
cards.back: Amplify cognition using computer-supported, interactive visual representations of abstract data.

cards.front: What type of data is scientific visualisation mainly concerned with?
cards.back: Spatial, physically based data with an inherent spatial mapping.

cards.front: What type of data is information visualisation mainly concerned with?
cards.back: Abstract data that does not have an inherent spatial mapping.

cards.front: Why does abstract data create a design challenge in InfoVis?
cards.back: Because the designer must decide how to map the data to visual form.

cards.front: When is visualisation especially useful compared with pure computational analysis?
cards.back: When questions are less targeted, many questions are possible, or the goal is to augment human capabilities.

cards.front: Why is interactivity important in information visualisation?
cards.back: Large or complex data cannot all be shown at once, and a single view usually shows only one aspect.

cards.front: What is Shneiderman’s Visual Information Seeking Mantra?
cards.back: Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand.

cards.front: What is sonification?
cards.back: Representing data through sound.

cards.front: What is data physicalisation?
cards.back: A physical artefact whose geometry or material properties encode data.

cards.front: Name the main stages of the visualisation pipeline.
cards.back: Raw data, data representation, visual representation, visual presentation, and view.

cards.front: What does data transformation do in the visualisation pipeline?
cards.back: It converts raw data into a structured data representation ready for visualisation.

cards.front: What is a data representation?
cards.back: Structured, tidy, machine-readable data ready to be visualised.

cards.front: What is visual mapping?
cards.back: The mapping from data attributes to marks and visual variables in a visual representation.

cards.front: What does presentation transformation consider?
cards.back: Display resolution, layout, arrangement, size, and possible interactions.

cards.front: What is the view in the visualisation pipeline?
cards.back: The rendered visualisation visible to the user, which can change through interaction.

cards.front: What are data semantics?
cards.back: The real-world meaning of the data: what a data point actually represents.

cards.front: Why do data semantics and data type matter in visualisation design?
cards.back: They influence the choice of visual representation.

cards.front: What is a categorical attribute?
cards.back: A discrete attribute with no intrinsic ordering.

cards.front: What operations make sense for categorical attributes?
cards.back: Same as and not the same as.

cards.front: What is an ordinal attribute?
cards.back: A discrete attribute with an implicit, well-defined ordering.

cards.front: Do mathematical operations generally make sense for ordinal attributes?
cards.back: No. Ranking makes sense, but arithmetic generally does not.

cards.front: What is a quantitative attribute?
cards.back: A measurement of magnitude where mathematical operations make sense.

cards.front: What typical relations are useful for quantitative data?
cards.back: Ranking, ratios, and correlations.

cards.front: What are marks in visualisation?
cards.back: Basic graphical elements visible on paper or screen.

cards.front: Name the basic mark types discussed in the course.
cards.back: Point, line, and area.

cards.front: What is the expressiveness principle?
cards.back: The visual encoding should express all of, and only, the information in the dataset attributes.

cards.front: How should ordered data be encoded under the expressiveness principle?
cards.back: In a way that our perceptual system intrinsically senses as ordered.

cards.front: How should categorical data be encoded under the expressiveness principle?
cards.back: In a way that does not perceptually suggest ordering.

cards.front: What is the effectiveness principle?
cards.back: The most important attributes should be encoded with the most effective visual variables so they are most noticeable.

cards.front: What five issues are considered under effectiveness?
cards.back: Accuracy, discriminability, separability, popout, and grouping.

cards.front: Why is hue limited for discriminability?
cards.back: Only about seven hue distinctions can be made reliably.

cards.front: What does separability ask about visual variables?
cards.back: How one visual variable interacts or interferes with another.

cards.front: What does popout mean in visual encoding?
cards.back: How easily items that stand out can be identified.

cards.front: Which visual variable is strongest for seeing grouping/similarity?
cards.back: Position.

cards.front: What data does a scatterplot primarily show?
cards.back: At least two quantitative attributes.

cards.front: How does a scatterplot encode quantitative values?
cards.back: Using point marks positioned horizontally and vertically.

cards.front: What analysis tasks do scatterplots support well?
cards.back: Finding correlations, overviews, distributions, trends, outliers, and extremes.

cards.front: What is a scale limitation of scatterplots?
cards.back: With large datasets, distinguishing individual points becomes difficult.

cards.front: What extra data can a bubble chart add beyond a basic scatterplot?
cards.back: A third quantitative attribute by size and often a categorical attribute by hue.

cards.front: What is a scatterplot matrix used for?
cards.back: Exploring pairwise correlations across multiple quantitative attributes.

cards.front: What is a typical scale guideline for scatterplot matrices?
cards.back: Fewer than about 12 attributes and hundreds of data points.

cards.front: What type of attributes do parallel coordinates visualise?
cards.back: Multiple quantitative or ordinal attributes.

cards.front: In parallel coordinates, what indicates positive correlation?
cards.back: Roughly parallel lines between adjacent axes.

cards.front: In parallel coordinates, what indicates negative correlation?
cards.back: Crossing lines between adjacent axes.

cards.front: What tasks do parallel coordinates support well?
cards.back: Finding correlations, ranges, extremes, and outliers.

cards.front: Why is axis ordering important in parallel coordinates?
cards.back: Only relationships between nearby axes are easy to interpret, so ordering affects visible patterns.

cards.front: What scale is parallel coordinates best suited for?
cards.back: Hundreds of items, not thousands, and a moderate number of attributes, around 12.

cards.front: What type of data are streamgraphs appropriate for?
cards.back: Temporal data.

cards.front: What visualisation uses bars arranged radially around a circle?
cards.back: A radial bar chart.

cards.front: What three activity groups can visualisations support in Munzner’s task abstraction?
cards.back: Analyse, search, and query.

cards.front: What are the two high-level modes of analyse activity?
cards.back: Consume and produce.

cards.front: What are the three query-related activities?
cards.back: Identify, compare, and summarise.

cards.front: What are the four search activities supported by visualisation?
cards.back: Lookup, locate, browse, and explore.

cards.front: In search activity taxonomy, when is a user doing lookup?
cards.back: When both target identity and target location are known.

cards.front: In search activity taxonomy, when is a user doing locate?
cards.back: When the target identity is known but its location is unknown.

cards.front: In search activity taxonomy, when is a user doing browse?
cards.back: When the target location is known but the target identity is unknown.

cards.front: In search activity taxonomy, when is a user doing explore?
cards.back: When both target identity and target location are unknown.

cards.front: What does a visualisation with the purpose of discover support?
cards.back: Open-ended exploration of data.

cards.front: What does a visualisation with the purpose of present support?
cards.back: Communication of existing knowledge.

cards.front: For discovery-oriented visualisations, what should the design show?
cards.back: The data from different perspectives.

cards.front: What is derive as a produce activity?
cards.back: Calculating or creating new data attributes from existing data.

cards.front: What does the rule of thumb 'no unjustified 3D' warn against?
cards.back: Using 3D when it does not serve the data or task.

cards.front: What does 'resolution over immersion' prioritise?
cards.back: Readable, information-rich display over immersive presentation.

cards.front: What does the rule 'eyes beat memory' mean?
cards.back: Prefer designs where users can visually compare information rather than remember it.

cards.front: What does 'get it right in black and white' mean?
cards.back: The design should remain understandable without relying solely on colour.

cards.front: What does 'form follows function' mean in visualisation?
cards.back: Visual design choices should be driven by the task and purpose.

cards.front: What is an arc diagram?
cards.back: A 1D relation visualisation where entities are nodes along an axis and relationships are arcs.

cards.front: What are arc diagrams good for showing?
cards.back: Pairwise relationships.

cards.front: How can arc diagrams encode relationship strength?
cards.back: Through arc thickness, height, or colour.

cards.front: How are relations typically represented in node-link diagrams?
cards.back: Each data point is a mark, and relations are shown by connections between marks.

cards.front: What is a major limitation of circular node-link arrangements?
cards.back: With many nodes and connections, they get messy quickly.

cards.front: What problem does hierarchical edge bundling address?
cards.back: It reduces visual clutter in dense relationship diagrams.

cards.front: What do chord diagrams visualise?
cards.back: Relationships between and within groups of entities.

cards.front: In a chord diagram, what does each outer circle fragment represent?
cards.back: A group of entities.

cards.front: In a chord diagram, what does the size of an outer fragment indicate?
cards.back: Part-to-whole breakdown for that group.

cards.front: In a chord diagram, what does arc size encode?
cards.back: The importance or frequency of the relationship.

cards.front: What are Sankey diagrams especially useful for?
cards.back: Showing how categories compare and flow into other states or categories.

cards.front: What is a key strength of treemaps?
cards.back: They are highly scalable for showing hierarchical part-to-whole data.

cards.front: Do treemaps use adjacency or containment layout?
cards.back: Containment layout.

cards.front: What is data-ink?
cards.back: Ink or pixels used to represent data; it changes if the data changes.

cards.front: What is the data-ink ratio?
cards.back: The proportion of total ink or pixels devoted to data-driven information.

cards.front: What does Tufte recommend regarding the data-ink ratio?
cards.back: Maximise data-ink and erase non-data ink and redundant data-ink, within reason.

cards.front: What is chart junk?
cards.back: Visual embellishments not essentially necessary to understand the data.

cards.front: Why can excessive dark gridlines be chart junk?
cards.back: They add clutter and graphic activity unrelated to the data.

cards.front: Name two common forms of chart junk.
cards.back: Unnecessary 3D effects and texturing.

cards.front: What is the main caveat to removing all non-data ink?
cards.back: Some redundancy and non-data ink can improve understanding, sensemaking, or recall.

cards.front: In visualisation, colour can be treated as which separate visual variables?
cards.back: Luminance/value/brightness, saturation, hue, and transparency.

cards.front: What is RGB mainly used for?
cards.back: Digital displays.

cards.front: What type of colour model is RGB?
cards.back: An additive colour model.

cards.front: What type of colour model is CMY?
cards.back: A subtractive colour model.

cards.front: What does HSL stand for?
cards.back: Hue, saturation, and lightness.

cards.front: What type of data is luminance good for?
cards.back: Ordered data types.

cards.front: Why is luminance important for intricate shapes and text?
cards.back: It has high resolution and supports shape and edge detection.

cards.front: What affects the perceived luminance of non-contiguous regions?
cards.back: The surrounding background and contrast effects.

cards.front: What is the rule of thumb for using greyscale to encode numerical values?
cards.back: Avoid using greyscale for more than five numerical values.

cards.front: What does saturation define?
cards.back: The purity or colourfulness of a hue.

cards.front: What type of data is saturation good for?
cards.back: Ordered data types.

cards.front: Why should saturation levels be used cautiously for small marks?
cards.back: Saturation is harder to distinguish in small regions.

cards.front: What type of data is hue good for?
cards.back: Categorical data, especially for showing groupings.

cards.front: Why should hue not normally encode ordered data?
cards.back: Hue has no implicit perceptual ordering.

cards.front: What is the rule of thumb for the number of hues?
cards.back: Do not use many more than seven different hues.

cards.front: What is transparency as a visual encoding?
cards.back: Encoding information by decreasing mark opacity from opaque to see-through.

cards.front: Is transparency separable from other colour variables?
cards.back: No. It strongly interacts with luminance and saturation.

cards.front: What is a major perceptual problem with the standard rainbow colourmap?
cards.back: It is perceptually non-linear.

cards.front: Name the seven interaction intentions from Yi et al.
cards.back: Select, explore/navigate, reconfigure, encode, abstract/elaborate/zoom, filter, and connect.

cards.front: What is the intention of select interaction?
cards.back: To mark something as interesting.

cards.front: Name two ways a visualisation can show feedback after selection.
cards.back: Changing colour, outline, size, or adding connecting lines.

cards.front: What is the intention of explore/navigate interaction?
cards.back: To show something new or change viewpoint.

cards.front: What is the intention of reconfigure interaction?
cards.back: To show the data in a different arrangement.

cards.front: What is the intention of encode interaction?
cards.back: To show a different visual representation or alter the visual encoding.

cards.front: What is the intention of abstract/elaborate/zoom interaction?
cards.back: To show more or less detail.

cards.front: Name two forms of details-on-demand.
cards.back: Side-by-side views, pop-up views, or focus-and-context views.

cards.front: What are Cairo’s three broad strategies for misleading through visualisation?
cards.back: Hiding relevant data, displaying too much data, and using graphic forms in inappropriate ways.

cards.front: What does data provenance involve in visualisation?
cards.back: Being transparent about data sources, references, context, and data collection.

cards.front: What is aleatory uncertainty?
cards.back: Irreducible randomness inherent in a process.

cards.front: What is epistemic uncertainty?
cards.back: Uncertainty from lack of knowledge that could theoretically be reduced with more information.

cards.front: What is ontological uncertainty?
cards.back: Uncertainty about how accurately the modelling describes reality.

cards.front: Name two visualisations that summarise uncertainty using intervals or summaries.
cards.back: Error bars, box plots, or icon arrays.

cards.front: Name two visualisations that show distributions for uncertainty.
cards.back: Gradient plots, quantile dot plots, violin plots, hypothetical outcome plots, or ensemble plots.

cards.front: What is a limitation of error bars?
cards.back: They summarise data and can lead to misinterpretation.

cards.front: How can axes mislead in visualisation?
cards.back: Obscuring or truncating axes can exaggerate or distort patterns.

cards.front: Why can inappropriate 3D effects be misleading?
cards.back: They can obscure the data.

cards.front: Name the six principles of data feminism.
cards.back: Rethink boundaries, embrace pluralism, examine power and aspire to empowerment, consider context, legitimise embodiment and affect, make labour visible.

cards.front: What does data feminism emphasise in visualisation?
cards.back: That data, design, and communities of use are intertwined, and design decisions expose assumptions.

cards.front: What does 'rethink binaries' ask designers to do?
cards.back: Use representational strategies based on multiplicity rather than fixed binaries.

cards.front: What does 'embrace pluralism' emphasise?
cards.back: Considering whose voices, perspectives, and subject positions are included or excluded.

cards.front: What does 'make labour visible' involve?
cards.back: Crediting those responsible for data collection, digitisation, cleaning, maintenance, and other project work.

cards.front: According to Correll, what are three ethical obligations of visualisation researchers?
cards.back: Make the invisible visible, collect data with empathy, and challenge structures of power.

cards.front: What is the first recommendation in the Do No Harm Guide?
cards.back: Critically examine your data.

cards.front: What language guidance appears in the Do No Harm Guide?
cards.back: Use people-first language.

cards.front: What is a data comic?
cards.back: A sequence of panels where text and images, including data and non-data graphics, convey a series of messages.

cards.front: What are the four essential components of data comics?
cards.back: Visualisation, flow, narration, and words & pictures.

cards.front: What is scrollytelling?
cards.back: A digital storytelling technique combining interactive scrolling with visual and textual elements to create a structured, immersive experience.

cards.front: What are pie charts typically used to show?
cards.back: Part-to-whole relationships or proportions of a total.

cards.front: What is a major weakness of pie charts?
cards.back: It is difficult to accurately compare angles or areas, especially with similar-sized slices.

cards.front: What is a common alternative to a pie chart for comparing parts of a whole?
cards.back: A bar chart or stacked bar chart.
